deep.reconstruction: There is no mathematics on this page. It is a draft from Riemann's natural-philosophical and psychological fragments. Related material appears in the 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts' printed in Weber's edition of the Werke, under 'Zur Psychologie und Metaphysik'. The page continues a discussion of Fechner, who is quoted: 'When the body of the lower soul dies, the higher soul takes it up, with its images of perception, into its life of memory.' Riemann concludes that, on Fechner's view, the souls of dead creatures form the elements of the Earth's soul-life. The numbered argument runs as follows. (1) Different thought-processes differ mainly in their temporal density or rate. If plants have souls, their hours and days would correspond to our seconds. The corresponding time-span for the Earth-soul, at least for its outward activity, might be many millennia. Accordingly, as far back as human historical memory reaches, the motions of the inorganic Earth are explicable by mechanical laws. (2) Riemann then asks what the elements of our own soul-life are. The simplest thing inner perception can distinguish is the simplest sensory presentation, e.g. a red point. Just as creatures' souls are the mental expression of a bodily process bounded in space and time, each elementary sensation is the mental expression of a bounded bodily process. Spatially, that process is the nerve process in a primitive (nerve) fibre. Temporally, it lasts a definite interval of about 1/10 to 1/9 of a second. Within these bounds we perceive no further differences: the impression is as if all parts of the process acted uniformly. He adds that every mental activity requires an expenditure of force, namely a consumption of nutrient substances. These facts are to be explained by a hypothesis: in our nervous systems, spatially and temporally delimited bodily processes occur whose purpose is to combine external influences into a mental unity. The next page continues the hypothesis: the carrier process is dissolved and excreted, while its mental content enters the soul and persists, which is how memory is explained. The only quantitative statement is the empirical estimate of the elementary perceptual time window, ≈0.1 s. The plant comparison implies a time-scale factor of roughly 3600 (an hour for a second) or 86400 (a day for a second); that inference is mine.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no derivation. The 1/10–1/9 s figure is a rough empirical estimate. It is consistent with 19th-century psychophysical values and with modern perceptual-moment estimates (~100 ms).
The remark that the plant/Earth time scales are 'hours and days' and 'millennia' is speculative Fechnerian analogy, not a derived result.

results.what: Elementary sensations are the mental expression of spatially and temporally bounded nerve processes, each lasting about 1/10–1/9 s, within which no temporal differences are perceived.
results.modern_name: Perceptual moment / temporal integration window (psychological present, ~100 ms)
results.usually_credited_to: Discussed by Fechner, Helmholtz, K.E. von Baer (time-scale relativity of organisms, 1860) and later by Stroud (1955, 'perceptual moment')

results.what: Different minds (plants, humans, Earth-soul) operate at different temporal densities, so that our seconds correspond to plants' hours.
results.modern_name: Relativity of subjective time scales (cf. von Baer's 'Augenblick')
results.usually_credited_to: K. E. von Baer (1860); G. T. Fechner (Zend-Avesta, 1851)

results.what: Mental acts consume energy (nutrients), and their bodily carriers are dissolved while their mental content persists; this is offered as a hypothesis for memory.
results.usually_credited_to: Riemann's published philosophical fragments (Werke, ed. Weber, 1876)

deep.surprise_reason: This is non-mathematical natural-philosophical text. Its themes (Fechner's Earth-soul, the elementary sensation lasting ~1/10 s, nerve processes as carriers of mental elements, memory) are well known from Riemann's published philosophical fragments in the Gesammelte Werke.

checkable.asserts: The stated window runs from 0.1 s to about 0.111 s.
The width of the estimated range is about 0.011 s.
'Hours for plants are seconds for us' corresponds to a time-scale factor of about 3600 (my inference).

transcription_corrections: Line on the Earth's inorganic motions: the interlinear insertion appears to be 'wohl', not 'nicht'. The sense is 'alle Bewegungen des unorganischen Erdkörpers wohl aus mechanischen Gesetzen zu erklären' (explicable by mechanical laws), consistent with the argument about the Earth-soul's slow time scale.
'so mussten Stunden und Tage' should probably read 'so müssten'.
'zeitliche Dichtheit[?]' is uncertain; it may be 'Dichtigkeit'. The sense is temporal density or rate.

'in [-der-] {+dem+} Ende[?] einer Primitivfaser' is uncertain in the image. In the later version it reads 'räumlich den Nervenprocess in (...) einer Primitivfaser'. The bracketed insertion is illegible and 'verschiedenen Enden' is doubtful.
'Ebenso[?] nun' is plausible; the image reads approximately 'Ebenso nun, wie die Seelen der Geschöpfe ...'.
